**What the US market is arguing about, Thursday Nov. 19, 2026 (as of 8:20 PM CT)**

Stocks fell hard on Thursday. The S&P 500 lost 2.02% to 7,175.83, its sixth straight decline. The Dow dropped about 1,100 points to 49,097, its first close below 50,000 since June. The Nasdaq fell 2.25%. Breadth was very bad, with about 446 decliners to 37 advancers and every sector down. The VIX rose about 16% to roughly 28, and CNN's Fear & Greed gauge sits near 19 (extreme fear). Closing figures come from [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/18/stock-market-today-live-updates.html) and [The Wall Street Republic](https://thewallstreetrepublic.substack.com/p/anthropic-closes-at-9717-s-and-p). Some details below rest on a single source or a live blog that changed during the day.

**1. The Anthropic IPO as an AI-positioning event (the main story)**
- It was the largest IPO on record. It raised about $81B at $83 a share, opened at $111.50 and closed at $97.17. That is up 17% from the offer price but about 13% below the first trade.
- The bull argument is that this puts a public price on AI value, about a $1.75T market cap. The bear argument is that it marks a top and pulls cash from other AI stocks.
- Reports say retail investors sold single stocks, AMD especially, to fund Anthropic purchases. Retail got about 15% of the deal, versus a typical 5% to 10%.
- The indexes hit their session lows soon after Anthropic began trading, which fits the "funding trade" story.
- Alphabet's reaction is a live question. A Motley Fool headline says Alphabet fell as the debut put a fresh value on Google's stake. I couldn't confirm the size of the move.

**2. Nvidia: a strong quarter overwhelmed by worries**
- The Nov. 17 results were strong. Revenue was $115.8B, up 103%. The Q4 guide of about $130B beat estimates, and there is a $150B buyback.
- The stock still closed at $145.98, down 3.3%, and is down roughly 28% this month. It opened up about 4.7% and reversed.
- The worries are these:
  - Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on Nov. 12, and the board says he won't be reinstated.
  - A reported SEC probe and shareholder lawsuits.
  - Tighter export rules, including on remote access to chips by Chinese firms.
  - Whether the AI buildout can justify its pace.
  - Fear that an incoming Democratic-led Congress will regulate AI.
- Bulls point to an RSI near 20 (deeply oversold) and the fundamentals. Morgan Stanley trimmed its target to $260 but kept Overweight.

**3. AMD short attack and the chip complex**
- AMD fell about 7.7% to $489 after Hunterbrook Capital disclosed a short position and alleged that a blacklisted Chinese server maker kept receiving AMD firmware. AMD denies it.
- Micron reversed from up 7.8% intraday to down 2.1%, which shows how fragile the AI rallies are.

**4. Rates: the Fed may be hiking, not cutting**
- One source says futures fully price a quarter-point hike at the Dec. 9 meeting. It says Waller floated a possible 50bp hike and that Wednesday's FOMC minutes were hawkish. I found only this one source, so check it before relying on it.
- The 10-year yield is about 5.04%, the 2-year about 4.76% and the 30-year about 5.40%. The Philly Fed prices-paid index jumped to its highest since June 2022, and the Philly Fed headline index fell to 6.3. Jobless claims were about 203k.
- The argument is whether this is a stagflation-lite setup or a hawkish Fed over a still-strong economy. High long yields pressure valuations in general and AI stocks in particular.

**5. Guidance disappointments in consumer and software**
- The pattern is that in-line or beating results were punished for soft outlooks.
- Williams-Sonoma fell 15% (guidance only reiterated, Q4 cost pressure). Intuit and Ross Stores reportedly fell about 11% and 7% after hours on weak guides. Walmart fell about 1% despite raising its full-year view, because that implies a softer Q4.
- Consumer discretionary was the worst sector, down about 2.8%.
- Counterpoint: Walmart reported resilient spending, with e-commerce up 17%. Palo Alto Networks rose about 6.4% on a beat and raise, and cybersecurity was the one bright spot.

**6. Other threads**
- Oil: WTI fell about 3% on some measures as Strait of Hormuz shipments returned to roughly pre-war levels. Another source had oil roughly flat at WTI $83 and Brent $92, so the two accounts conflict.
- Gold fell 3.7% in one report, which suggests broad deleveraging rather than a rotation into safety.
- UnitedHealth is down about 18% over five days, with a 5% drop on Thursday.
- Politics: an incoming Democratic-led Congress is a new worry for AI and tech regulation.

**What to watch next**
- Whether Anthropic holds above its $83 offer price and what that does to Alphabet and Amazon.
- Whether AI stocks bounce from oversold levels or the selling spreads.
- The Dec. 9 FOMC meeting and further Fed speakers.
- Intuit and Ross on Friday's open.

**The story**
- **Defensive rotation.** Insurers have behaved as a safe haven when AI and tech names sell off. Bloomberg reported on July 28, 2026 that an insurance gauge closed at a record as traders left AI-exposed stocks for defensives. Coverage of Nov 16 and 17 shows the same setup: Nasdaq -2.5% and S&P 500 -1.9% on Nov 16, then S&P 500 -1% on Nov 17 to 7,340.5. Your screen's pattern (group +1.5% vs XLF, all 10 above their 50-day averages, S&P -2.0% today) fits that rotation. It looks like a flight to low-beta stocks, not a change in insurer fundamentals.
- **Soft pricing is the long-run headwind.**
  - Marsh reports global commercial rates fell 5% in Q3 2026, the ninth straight quarterly decline. US property fell about 10%, and casualty rose about 1%.
  - Baldwin's index shows commercial property down 8.0% in Q3, flat against Q2's 8.1% decline. Commercial auto pricing eased to 2.9%, its lowest reading since the index began.
  - Alera, citing The Council, calls the first half of 2026 the softest market since 2017. Swiss Re and Willis expect softness to continue through 2027, with reinsurance down by double digits.
  - Umbrella and excess casualty are still firm: Baldwin shows umbrella up 5.6%, and Alera projects about +11%.
  - Lockton warns that liability loss costs are outpacing pricing.
- **Earnings are strong for now.** One headline reports a US P&C underwriting gain of $31.7B (I saw only the headline, not the period). The market is paying for margins that are peaking, not growing.

**What could move the group over the next 1-10 sessions**
- **Up:** more equity weakness in AI and tech, which keeps the defensive bid going. Yields falling would also help. A quiet catastrophe period would support the group.
- **Down:** a sharp bounce in tech would reverse the rotation, and the spread is stretched (+2.3 standard deviations, a 20-day high), so mean reversion is a real risk. A late-year catastrophe event such as a winter storm or wildfire would hit personal-lines names (ALL, PGR, TRV) hardest. Further soft-market headlines, including the December reinsurance renewal commentary, hit the commercial and reinsurance names (CB, ACGL, EG, WRB).
- **Within the group:** BRK B was the laggard today (-0.4%). It is a conglomerate, not a pure insurer, and it trades more with the broad market. PGR was the best (+0.7%).

**What I could not confirm:** the cause of today's move, any company-specific news for the 10 names, and the Q3 earnings reactions. I did not check upcoming dated catalysts.

**Story:** Valvoline reported fiscal Q4 2026 results today. The stock rose 10.4% on a day the S&P fell 2.0%. The move reads as a relief and guidance rally: the headline EPS only matched estimates, but sales were strong, FY27 guidance looks solid, and the buyback was enlarged.

**Q4 figures (quarter ended Sep 30, per the 8-K):**
- Revenue rose 22% to $554.1M, in line with the consensus MarketBeat cites ($555.3M).
- System-wide same-store sales rose 9.4%.
- System-wide store sales rose 20% to $1.1B.
- 61 stores were added in the quarter.
- Adjusted EBITDA rose 10% to $143.6M.
- Adjusted EPS was $0.42, down 7% from a year ago. It met estimates.
- Reported EPS was $0.08, down 60%, after large one-time charges: $20.3M legacy and separation costs, $16.7M pension expense, $6.5M IT transition and material weakness remediation, and $5.3M debt extinguishment.

**Full year:** Revenue was $2.06B, up 21%. Same-store sales rose 7.9%, the 20th straight year of growth. Adjusted EPS rose 11% to $1.76. Free cash flow was $204M. There are 2,517 stores and debt is $1.6B.

**FY27 guidance:**
- Same-store sales growth of 5–7%.
- 190–220 new stores.
- Revenue of $2.25–2.35B.
- Adjusted EBITDA of $595–625M, about 7% growth at the midpoint.
- Adjusted EPS of $1.85–2.05, about 8% growth at the midpoint.
- Capex of $245–265M.
- Buyback authorization raised to $500M.
- The outlook assumes product costs stay elevated and supply is stable.

**Why it probably rallied:**
- The stock was likely depressed going in. Benzinga's headline (seen on a Stocktwits news list) says shares rose on "strong store growth offsetting margin pressure."
- Same-store sales of 9.4% beat the roughly 5% market expectation Stifel cited back in March.
- Guidance was no worse than feared.
- The $500M buyback is large relative to a market cap of roughly $4.7B. I estimated that cap from the 36.84 close and an assumed share count near 127M. I did not verify the count.
- Cost pass-through is the bear point. Stifel's March upgrade (target $42) argued Valvoline can pass base-oil cost increases through to customers.

**What could move it over the next few sessions:**
- **Analyst target raises and upgrades.** These are likely Friday. Past upgrades such as Stifel's moved the stock about 5% in a day.
- **Post-earnings drift versus fade.** After a 10% gap the stock sits just under its 20-day high of 36.92. A break above 36.92 would continue the move. A failure there would suggest a fade.
- **Market direction.** The S&P fell 2.0% today and the stock rose anyway. That gives it a relative-strength premium that could unwind if the market rebounds, or hold if the selloff continues.
- **Margin and EPS quality.** Adjusted EPS fell year over year and GAAP EPS fell 60%. Skeptics may point to those one-time items.
- **Oil and base-oil costs.** These are the main macro sensitivity.

**After-hours:** The stock was 36.58 at 7:00 PM CT, down 0.7%. That is mild profit-taking, not a reversal.

- I couldn't confirm the date of the Benzinga piece, and I couldn't read it because the page returned 403.

**Bottom line:** The quarter was fine and guidance was only reiterated. The stock was hit because the print left no cushion: revenue slightly missed, Pottery Barn slowed, and the year's guidance leaves little room for the holiday quarter. The selloff looks like a de-rating on a stock that had run up into earnings, not a broken business. The pre-earnings close of about $260 comes from one article; it matches 220.66 being down 15.2%.

**What was reported (quarter ended Nov 1, from the 8-K release)**
- Net revenue was $1.99B, up 5.8%, against a roughly $2.0B consensus, so a small miss.
- Comparable brand revenue rose 5.1%, against 4.0% a year ago.
  - Williams Sonoma brand: +6.8%.
  - West Elm: +7.0%.
  - Pottery Barn: only +1.8%.
  - Pottery Barn Kids and Teen: +2.9%.
- Non-GAAP EPS was $2.19 against about $2.18 expected, a one-cent beat. Non-GAAP operating margin was 17.4%, up 40 bps.
- GAAP EPS of $2.38 includes a $29M IEEPA tariff refund (about $0.19 per share). The company excludes it from non-GAAP, and it expects no more refunds in Q4.
- Inventory was $1.64B, up 7.3%, which is faster than sales growth of 5.8%.
- Cash was $992M. The company bought back $163M of stock in the quarter.

**Why the stock fell (my read, since the sources treat causes as inference)**
1. **Pottery Barn:** Management deliberately pulled back on markdowns, especially seasonal and back-to-school goods, to sell more at full price. The result was a 1.8% comp. Management says this is ongoing.
2. **Guidance only reiterated:**
   - The full-year figures were net revenue +4.7% to +7.2%, comps +4.0% to +6.5%, and non-GAAP operating margin 17.8% to 18.2%.
   - Year-to-date non-GAAP operating margin is about 17.0% (Briefing.com), so hitting the range needs a strong holiday quarter.
   - Q4 laps a roughly 160 bps shrink benefit from last year. Lower tariff costs are expected to largely offset it.
3. **Costs:** Diesel was up more than 60% year over year. It cost about 75 bps in the quarter, and management flagged up to $60M of extra diesel expense for the year. Guidance assumes oil stays at current levels.
4. **Macro and demand:** Management said housing got worse during the quarter. Customers are buying later for holiday goods, and competitors are very promotional.
5. **Long-term targets:** Analysts pressed on why the press release dropped the long-term algorithm. Management said it is unchanged. Fiscal 2027 guidance comes in March.

**Analysts:** I found only target raises, with no cuts. Telsey went to $285 from $260 (Outperform) and Jefferies to $275 from $260 (Buy). UBS went to $265 from $247. The dates are unclear and may predate the print, so they may not reflect the reaction. Check for fresh post-print notes on Friday morning. These targets sit well above 220, so dip-buying support is plausible.

The stock closed in the bottom third of the day's range on 4.4 times normal volume, and after-hours was flat at 220.00. A break below the 200-day on follow-through selling is the bear case. Holding it and basing is the bounce case.
- **Holiday data:** Black Friday and Cyber Monday readouts, and retail peers' earnings. Peers in the same week or two could shift the sector tone.
- **Macro:** Oil and diesel prices, housing and mortgage-rate data, and tariff news. A tariff ruling or refund headlines could swing sentiment either way.
- **Overhang:** Large post-earnings gap-downs often see continued drift lower or a partial retrace. After a 15% one-day drop, the usual outcomes are a dead-cat bounce or slow drift near the 200-day.

**GLBE: research summary as of 8:25 PM CT, Thu 2026-11-19**

**The story**
Global-e runs cross-border e-commerce checkout for merchants, including Shopify stores. It handles duties, tax, payments and delivery on the merchant's behalf. Q3 2026 was reported on Nov 18 before the open. The results were strong, but the market sold the quality of the beat, not the headline numbers.

**Q3 numbers**
- **Growth:** GMV was $2.042B, up 35%. Revenue was $314.1M, up 42%, against a consensus of about $312.6M.
- **EPS:** Non-GAAP EPS was $0.37 against $0.23 expected. Adjusted EBITDA was $63.7M, with the margin at 20.3% against 18.7% a year earlier.
- **Operating costs:** Adjusted opex fell to 24.9% of revenue from 28.0%.
- **Free cash flow:** It was $66.4M, down from $73.6M.
- **Outlook:** Full-year guidance was raised, with GMV of $8.957B to $9.117B (about 38% growth). Q4 guidance is GMV of $3.085B to $3.245B, revenue of $464M to $488M and adjusted EBITDA of $113.5M to $123.5M. I found no Q4 consensus to compare against.
- **Buyback:** About $53M was repurchased in Q3. Roughly $446M remains under a $500M plan.

**Why it sold off (inferred from coverage, since no single cause was stated)**
- **Revenue beat:** It was tiny, about 0.5%, next to the large EPS beat.
- **Gross margin:** Non-GAAP gross margin fell to 44.8% from 46.3%. The CFO blamed mostly fuel surcharges that were paused in Q2 and Q3 and updated for Q4.
- **Passport mix:** The Passport acquisition is lower-margin. Fulfillment revenue grew 54% while higher-margin service-fee revenue grew 30%, and management said the mix differs from plan.
- **Take rates:** Service-fee take rates have declined because of the Managed Markets V2 migration and volume-tiered pricing for larger merchants. Management expects them to be "quite stable" from here.
- **Softer growth signals:** Same-store sales cooled from the first half, partly from FX. Q3 GMV fell versus Q2 because promotions pulled activity forward. Duty drawback adoption is slower, which management tied to the Supreme Court IEEPA tariff ruling.
- **Expectations:** The stock was at its 2026 high near $42.49 on Nov 9 and was $39.81 going into the print. Investors want proof that growth can accelerate into 2027 without further margin pressure.

**Price action**
- **Nov 18:** The stock was down as much as 13.8% pre-market, to about $34.31, and recovered to about -4.5% at the close.
- **Nov 19:** It fell another 7.7% to $35.10. I found no news or analyst action explaining Nov 19. I could not find any 2026 analyst price-target changes either, because the searches returned only 2025 items. The second leg down looks like continued selling of an expensive stock that broke down, not new information. That is my inference.

**What could move it over the next 1 to 10 sessions**
- **Analyst notes:** Target changes and rating changes will likely land over the next few days. These could either confirm the selling or support a bounce, since the fundamentals (EPS beat, raised guidance, 54% EBITDA growth) are intact.
- **Mean reversion:** RSI is 31 and the stock is about 17% below its pre-earnings price, so a bounce is plausible. A multi-day post-earnings drift lower is also plausible, because the stock is below both its 50-day and 200-day averages and the last two sessions were heavy selling.
- **Buyback:** Management has a large remaining authorization and could be a buyer on weakness. That is a modest support, not a catalyst.
- **Macro and tariffs:** Tariff and de minimis news, Shopify or e-commerce read-throughs and holiday cross-border volume reports could all move the stock.
- **No scheduled company catalyst:** I found none in the window. The next earnings report is months away.

**What happened.** Intuit reported fiscal Q1 2027 after the close today. It beat on the headline numbers and cut Credit Karma, so the selloff is about guidance and the AI narrative, not about the quarter. The stock has already fallen a long way. Per the August coverage it was down about 47% year to date, and that was before today's drop.

- **Quarter:** Revenue was $4.35B, up 12%, above the top of Intuit's guide. Non-GAAP EPS was $2.91, up 56%, with non-GAAP now including stock compensation. Business Solutions rose 15% (Online Ecosystem +20%).
- **Credit Karma (the trigger):** Revenue grew 9%, but management said it was "below our internal expectations for both revenue and engagement." FY27 Credit Karma growth is now 3-7%. It was the only piece of full-year revenue guidance that changed, and the release doesn't give the prior range. Two reasons were given:
  - Higher interest rates hit growth late in the quarter.
  - Consumers are "increasingly starting in AI-powered experiences" to find financial products, a faster shift than Intuit expected. This hits the main bear thesis of AI tools cutting out Intuit.
- **Guidance:**
  - FY27 revenue is $23.08-23.37B, up 8-9%.
  - FY27 non-GAAP EPS of $22.88-23.12 was reiterated.
  - Q2 revenue is up 6-7%, with non-GAAP EPS of $3.17-3.22.
  - Consumer revenue is guided down mid-single digits in Q2, because price-sensitive filers are choosing free options earlier. About $30M of refund-transfer revenue also shifts from Q2 to Q3.
- **Mailchimp:** Intuit is selling it to Bending Spoons for about $3.68B ($3.31B cash, $368M in Bending Spoons stock). Closing is expected in early calendar 2027, pending regulatory approvals. Proceeds are earmarked for buybacks in FY27, and guidance excludes the sale.
- **Capital return:** Buybacks were $1.5B in the quarter (up 73%), with $6.4B authorization left. The dividend was raised 15% to $1.38.

**Price.** One TradingView/Seeking Alpha item had the stock down about 12% at $272.78 after hours. That is deeper than your 7:00 PM CT print of 279.74 (down 9.8%). It suggests the move may have extended lower, but I couldn't confirm the timing or the price. The 52-week low of 250.56 is about 8% below 272.78, and August's retail chatter was calling for a test near $250.

**What could move it over the next 1-10 sessions**
- **Tomorrow's open:** The gap and where it holds relative to 250.56 matter most. Heavy volume and a sentiment swing on the August drop (retail turned extremely bullish) suggest two-sided trading.
- **Analyst moves:** Price-target cuts are likely. Some will note the beat and reiterated EPS as a "kitchen-sink" reset. I found no analyst reaction yet.
- **Buyback support:** $1.5B a quarter, plus Mailchimp proceeds after closing, gives some support. The proceeds come after the next few sessions, though.
- **Rates:** The Credit Karma cut is tied to interest rates, so rate moves feed back into the stock.

- **Valuation bounce:** EPS guidance of about $23 implies roughly 12x at 272-280. That could draw dip buyers, as in August.

**Net read.** A beat plus a small, specific guidance cut, at multi-year lows and below both moving averages, is a setup where the direction after a gap is uncertain. Continuation lower is plausible because the AI-disruption narrative is confirmed again. A bounce is plausible because the EPS guide held.
